numbers.headline: Researchers grouped about 12 in 100 adults as ‘recovery’ from porn or sex problems; it does not count who got free.
numbers.mirror: You wonder whether a porn problem ever fades by itself.
numbers.counted: Israeli men and women whose answers showed likely porn or sex problems

basis.design: community group surveyed four times; the researchers’ statistics sorted people into four groups by their answers in 2018 and 2022, and the researchers named the groups
basis.who: Jewish adults in Israel aged 18 to 70, from a community sample; men and women are counted together, and no split by sex is reported; how much they watched is not reported
basis.n: 1,182 adults sorted into four groups: 138 in the group named ‘recovery’, 42 ‘chronic’, 50 ‘delayed onset’, 952 ‘no disorder’
basis.when: surveys in 2018 and 2022, before the war that began in October 2023, which the later surveys covered; published 2026
basis.measured: Questionnaires for a likely porn problem and a likely compulsive sex problem, at both surveys; the groups count the two together. ‘Recovery’ and ‘chronic’ are the researchers’ names for the groups.

numbers.caveat: The second survey came four years after the first. Questionnaire answers, not a doctor’s check, and porn and sex problems are counted together. The researchers’ statistics drew and named the groups, so this does not show that each of the 138 had a problem in 2018 or is free of it now, or that anyone tried to quit. This is not a count of people who got free.
numbers.weak: A model’s grouping, not a count

ref.cite: Efrati Y, Shmulewitz D, Skvirsky V, Vider M, Kor A, Lev-Ran S, Mikulincer M (2026). Longitudinal study of probable compulsive sexual behavior disorder and problematic pornography use profiles: their prospective impact on psychopathology during wartime. Addictive Behaviors, article 108589.

numbers.headline: Of men who wanted help for their porn use, 40 in 100 had already tried to quit completely four or more times.
numbers.mirror: You’ve tried four times and think nobody fails that often.
numbers.counted: men who said they wanted porn help, not checked by a doctor

basis.who: men who watch porn and said they wanted help for it, found mostly through Craigslist ads; average age 33; 132 of the 186 scored at or above a checklist line for likely out-of-control sexual behaviour; about 80 in 100 of all men surveyed watched at least weekly
basis.n: 186 men who wanted help for their porn use (of 1,298 surveyed)
basis.where: USA, Canada and other English-speaking countries
basis.measured: Past tries to quit porn completely and to cut back: none, 1 to 3, or 4 or more. Among men who did not want help, 6 in 100 had tried to quit four or more times.

numbers.caveat: One survey at one moment, so it cannot say whether these men got free later or how many tries quitting usually takes: it counts tries by men still struggling. Volunteers who answered an ad. The same men: 46 in 100 had tried to cut back, not quit, four or more times.
numbers.weak: Men still struggling, not men free

ref.cite: Kraus SW, Martino S, Potenza MN (2016). Clinical characteristics of men interested in seeking treatment for use of pornography. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 5:169-178.
ref.quote: Quit attempts with porn 0 attempts (“never”) 25.3 75.0 251.05 <0.001 1-to-3 past attempts 34.4 19.2 4+ past attempts 40.3 5.8

numbers.headline: At the end of 12 ACT talk-therapy sessions, 54 in 100 men had stopped porn completely.
numbers.mirror: You wonder whether therapy can get a man fully off porn.
numbers.counted: men in a therapy trial for problem porn use

basis.design: a trial that split men by chance between ACT therapy and a waiting list; this figure counts both groups once the waiting-list men had their therapy too
basis.who: adult men with problematic internet porn use; all but one were Latter-day Saints; how much they watched before therapy is not reported
basis.measured: Self-reported porn viewing at the end of 12 one-to-one sessions of acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), which trains you to let urges come and go without acting on them. While one group waited, average viewing was 93% lower with therapy and 21% lower on the waiting list.

numbers.caveat: This figure counts all men after they had therapy, so there are no untreated men to compare it with. There was no comparison therapy, so it does not show ACT beats other help. Three months later, 35 in 100 had stopped completely.
numbers.weak: No comparison count; 26 men, almost all one church

ref.cite: Crosby JM, Twohig MP (2016). Acceptance and commitment therapy for problematic internet pornography use: a randomized trial. Behavior Therapy 47:355-366.
ref.quote: Complete cessation was seen in 54% of participants at posttreatment and at least a 70% reduction was seen in 93% of participants.

numbers.headline: Of 104 men keeping an online journal while quitting porn, 53 in 100 wrote about slipping at least once.
numbers.mirror: You slipped and think men serious about quitting never do.
numbers.counted: men on a quit-porn forum, most calling themselves addicted

basis.design: study of online quitting journals, with no comparison group
basis.who: men aged 18 to 63 on the Reboot Nation forum; 80 of the 104 called themselves addicted to porn; how much they watched is not reported
basis.measured: Slips the men wrote about, and how long each journal's attempt ran. Only journals covering 7 days to 12 months were picked. At least 86 in 100 were also trying to stop masturbating.

numbers.caveat: Many men just stopped writing, so nobody knows how their attempts ended, and the study does not say when in an attempt the slips came. Slips the men did not write about are not counted. About half the attempts seemed to run 7 to 30 days, judged from the men's own day counts or the dates of their posts. Men who journal in public may differ from men who quit quietly.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: More than half of the sample (n = 55) reported at least one lapse during their abstinence attempt.

numbers.headline: Asked to stop porn for a week, 45 in 100 students in a trial watched at least once.
numbers.mirror: You slipped in your first week and think that makes you weak.
numbers.counted: students who watch porn often, mostly women, most not hooked

basis.design: a trial that split students by chance into a stop group and a keep-watching group
basis.who: psychology undergraduates who watched porn 3 or more times a week; 64 in 100 were women, average age 21
basis.n: 86 asked to stop for 7 days (of 176 in the trial)
basis.measured: Each night for 7 days: craving, good and bad mood, withdrawal symptoms, and any porn use.

numbers.caveat: Mostly women students, most with no wish to quit, and slipping cost them nothing. A real, chosen quit attempt may go differently.
numbers.weak: Students, mostly women, mostly not hooked

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Justice LV, Fernandez EF, Griffiths MD (2023). Effects of a 7-day pornography abstinence period on withdrawal-related symptoms in regular pornography users: a randomized controlled study. Archives of Sexual Behavior 52:1819-1840.
ref.quote: nearly half (45.4%) of participants in the abstinence group reported using pornography at least once during the experimental period

numbers.headline: Of Polish students still watching porn, 51 in 100 had tried at least once to stop, and gone back.
numbers.mirror: You’ve tried to quit and failed, and think few people do.
numbers.counted: ordinary students who still watch porn, not checked for addiction

basis.design: one-time online survey; students chose to take part
basis.who: university students aged 18 to 26 who currently watch porn, most often once a week, about 11 in 100 daily; about 60 in 100 were women
basis.n: 4,260 students who still watch (1,740 of them men)
basis.measured: Ever making at least one attempt to stop using porn.

numbers.caveat: These are people still watching, so their attempts did not stick. It cannot say how many attempts quitting usually takes. Ordinary students, not checked for addiction, and about 60 in 100 were women.

ref.cite: Dwulit AD, Rzymski P (2019). Prevalence, patterns and self-perceived effects of pornography consumption in Polish university students: a cross-sectional study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 16:1861.
ref.quote: 51.0% admitted to making at least one attempt to give up using it with no difference in the frequency of these attempts between males and females

numbers.headline: Students who watched daily and scored high for problem use craved more on a 7-day break than peers who kept watching.
numbers.mirror: You wonder what a week off porn will feel like.
numbers.counted: regular porn users, most not hooked

basis.design: a trial that split students by chance into a stop group and a keep-watching group; the result for daily users comes from an extra check the researchers had not planned
basis.who: psychology undergraduates who watched porn 3 or more times a week; 64 in 100 were women, average age 21
basis.n: 176: 86 asked to stop for 7 days, 90 who kept watching; about 34 of the 176 (19 in 100) watched daily or more
basis.measured: Each night for 7 days: craving, good and bad mood, and withdrawal symptoms, compared between the two groups after allowing for starting scores.

numbers.caveat: Most were not hooked: 85 in 100 scored below the line for a likely problem, 90 in 100 had no wish to quit, and 45 in 100 of the stop group watched anyway. Even the ‘high’ problem score in the extra check was below that line. That result rests on few people. Mood and withdrawal showed no clear difference, but the researchers say there were too few people to rule out smaller effects. Nothing was measured after day 7.
numbers.weak: Students, mostly not hooked, one week

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Justice LV, Fernandez EF, Griffiths MD (2023). Effects of a 7-day pornography abstinence period on withdrawal-related symptoms in regular pornography users: a randomized controlled study. Archives of Sexual Behavior 52:1819-1840.
ref.quote: an abstinence effect on craving was found at high levels of PPU only once past 4-week FPU reached the threshold of daily use

numbers.headline: Of 42 men on a quit-porn forum with erection trouble at the start, 50 in 100 wrote of at least some improvement.
numbers.mirror: You hope quitting porn will fix your erections.
numbers.counted: men on a quit-porn forum who said they had erection trouble

basis.design: study of online quitting journals, with no comparison group
basis.who: men aged 18 to 63 keeping a journal of a quit-porn attempt on the Reboot Nation forum; how much they watched is not reported
basis.n: 42 men who wrote about erection trouble at the start (of 104 journals)
basis.measured: What the men wrote about their erections during attempts lasting 7 days to 12 months.

numbers.caveat: Their own words, not a doctor's check, and nobody was compared with men who kept watching. The study does not say how the other 21 fared. The authors say men it helped were likelier to keep posting, and most were also stopping masturbation, so the change may not come from quitting porn alone. At most 32 of the 42 called themselves addicted. A three-sample study of porn and erections found no sign that porn causes erection trouble, and it did not check for medical causes; a doctor can.

ref.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
ref.quote: Of the 42 members who reported erectile difficulties at the outset of the abstinence attempt, half (n = 21) reported at least some improvements in erectile function

alsoRef.cite: Grubbs JB, Gola M (2019). Is pornography use related to erectile functioning? Results from cross-sectional and latent growth curve analyses. Journal of Sexual Medicine 16:111-125.
alsoRef.quote: the work relied exclusively on self-report methods, and did not control for medical covariates that may be related to the experience of ED

numbers.headline: Three months after ACT talk therapy ended, 35 in 100 men had stopped porn completely; 54 in 100 had at the end.
numbers.mirror: You fear it all comes back once the help stops.
numbers.counted: men in a therapy trial for problem porn use

basis.design: a trial that split men by chance between ACT therapy and a waiting list; 3-month check-up, both groups together after the waiting-list men had therapy
basis.who: adult men with problematic internet porn use; all but one were Latter-day Saints; how much they watched before therapy is not reported
basis.n: 26 men, both groups together; the study does not say how many were checked at 3 months
basis.measured: Self-reported porn viewing at the 3-month follow-up: 35 in 100 had stopped completely. Another measure, 74 in 100 watching at least 70% less than before therapy, counts watching less, so it is not used as the result here.

numbers.caveat: Nearly all from one church, self-report, only 3 months. Some progress faded: 54 in 100 had stopped completely at the end of therapy, 35 in 100 three months later. Quality of life was measured too; a 2022 review of the trial lists no change in it for the men in therapy.

ref.cite: Crosby JM, Twohig MP (2016). Acceptance and commitment therapy for problematic internet pornography use: a randomized trial. Behavior Therapy 47:355-366.
ref.quote: At the 3-month follow-up assessment, 35% of participants showed complete cessation, with 74% of participants showing at least 70% reduction in viewing.

alsoRef.cite: Antons S, Engel J, Briken P, Krüger THC, Brand M, Stark R (2022). Treatments and interventions for compulsive sexual behavior disorder with a focus on problematic pornography use: a preregistered systematic review. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 11:643-666.
alsoRef.quote: ↔ quality of life (TG: BL = post, CG: BL< post, BL < post)

numbers.headline: Of Polish students who had ever watched porn, 16 in 100 said they had stopped, men as often as women.
numbers.mirror: You doubt anyone really manages to stop watching porn.
numbers.counted: ordinary students who had ever watched porn, not addicts

basis.design: one-time online survey; students chose to take part
basis.who: university students aged 18 to 26 who had ever seen porn; about 60 in 100 were women; how much they had watched is not reported
basis.n: 5,083 students who had ever watched (2,079 men); 823 had stopped (339 men)
basis.measured: Saying they had successfully stopped using porn.

numbers.caveat: One-time survey; ‘stopped’ has no time frame, so some may have stopped recently. Most were never hooked. Says nothing about what improved afterwards.

ref.cite: Dwulit AD, Rzymski P (2019). Prevalence, patterns and self-perceived effects of pornography consumption in Polish university students: a cross-sectional study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 16:1861.
ref.quote: while the rest ( n = 823; 484 female and 339 male) reported to successfully cease its use

beliefs.limiting: I’ve watched porn since I was a teenager. It’s wired in. I’m stuck with it.
beliefs.counterpart: I can’t call it wired in until I’ve stayed off for three months. I’m doing it now.
beliefs.whenThought: Write the thought down, and next to it: “I can’t call it wired in until I’ve stayed off for three months.” Then put the phone in another room and do the next step of the plan below.
beliefs.test: One evening this week, spend your usual porn hour as a man already getting free: out with people, at the gym, or on a job you’ve put off. At bedtime, count the minutes of that hour you spent thinking about porn.
beliefs.proof: In men’s porn-quit journals, most by men who called themselves addicted, about 27 in 100 recorded a quit attempt lasting 3 months or more.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50(2):711-728.
refs.quote: Inferred duration of abstinence attempt 7 days–30 days 54 52.0 1 month–3 months 22 21.2 3 months–6 months 13 12.5 6 months–1 year 15 14.4

beliefs.limiting: Quitting means a brutal flatline and weeks of withdrawal.
beliefs.counterpart: Some men get a flat spell. Mostly, the hard part is the pull.
beliefs.whenThought: Write the thought down, and next to it: “Mostly, the hard part is the pull.” Still watching? Do the next step of the plan. Already off it? On a flat or hard day, text the person you told your date.
beliefs.test: Still watching? Take two days off porn this week. Already off it? Use your next two days. Each night, give the day one score from 0 (easy) to 10 (unbearable) and name what was hard: your body, or the pull. By the second night you’ll know which one it was.
beliefs.proof: In 104 men’s porn-quit journals, most by men who called themselves addicted, close to 33 in 100 wrote of a ‘flatline’, a spell of low sex drive.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
refs.quote: close to one-third of members reported that instead of experiencing increased sexual desire, they experienced diminished sexual desire during abstinence, which they called the “flatline.”

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.

beliefs.limiting: I need it to switch off. Nothing else works at the end of the day.
beliefs.counterpart: Porn is one way I switch off. It isn’t the only one I have.
beliefs.whenThought: When the thought comes at the end of the day, write next to it: “It isn’t the only way I switch off.” Then do one swap from step 2 for that hour: a walk, a shower or a call.
beliefs.test: On three evenings this week, when you’d reach for porn to switch off, switch off another way instead: a walk, a shower, a call. No porn those evenings. Rate the pull 0–10 before and after. Notice how much of the need the swap covered.
beliefs.proof: In 104 men’s porn-quit journals, most by men who called themselves addicted, more than 75 in 100 wrote of other ways to get through, such as exercise, going out, better sleep or changing how they thought.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
refs.quote: Because members had previously often relied on pornography use to regulate negative affect, uncomfortable emotions appeared to have become a conditioned cue for pornography use.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
refs.quote: Most members reported making use of various internal resources (i.e., cognitive and/or behavioral strategies) to aid their abstinence.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
refs.quote: “many” refers to between 50% and 75% of members, and “most” refers to more than 75% of members.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
refs.quote: Day-to-day behavioral strategies (e.g., exercising, meditating, socializing, keeping busy, going out more often, and having a healthier sleep routine) were incorporated as part of an overall lifestyle change

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.

beliefs.limiting: One quick look won’t hurt. I can handle it now.
beliefs.counterpart: I’ve tried keeping it to a little before. It didn’t stay little.
beliefs.whenThought: Write next to the thought: “It didn’t stay little.” Then treat it as the start of a binge: phone in another room, and you out of the room for 20 minutes.
beliefs.test: The next time “just one look” comes up this week, treat it as the start of a binge: put the phone in another room for 20 minutes. See whether “just one” is still asking when you come back.
beliefs.proof: Of men who said they wanted help with porn, 46 in 100 had already tried to cut back, not quit, four or more times.
beliefs.counted: men who said they wanted porn help, not checked by a doctor

refs.cite: Kraus SW, Martino S, Potenza MN (2016). Clinical characteristics of men interested in seeking treatment for use of pornography. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 5:169-178.
refs.quote: Out of the 1,298 individuals surveyed, 14.3% (n = 186) reported a current interest in seeking treatment for use of pornography.

refs.cite: Kraus SW, Martino S, Potenza MN (2016). Clinical characteristics of men interested in seeking treatment for use of pornography. Journal of Behavioral Addictions 5:169-178.
refs.quote: Cut back attempts with porn 0 attempts (“never”) 12.9 65.5 216.04 <0.001 1-to-3 past attempts 40.9 23.4 4+ past attempts 46.2 11.2

beliefs.weak: No study of men checked for porn addiction

beliefs.limiting: I slipped again. I’m just someone who can’t quit.
beliefs.counterpart: A slip is one day. The days I kept still happened.
beliefs.whenThought: After a slip, write the thought down, and next to it: “A slip is one day. The days I kept still happened.” Then do what a kept day does next: shower, get dressed, get out of the house.
beliefs.test: If you slip this week, run the next day exactly like a kept day: same alarm, blocker on, plans as made. That evening, check what the slip cost: one day, or the whole attempt.
beliefs.proof: In men’s porn-quit journals, most by men who called themselves addicted, about 48 in 100 recorded a quit attempt of over a month, though many wrote of a slip along the way.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50(2):711-728.
refs.quote: 1 month–3 months 22 21.2 3 months–6 months 13 12.5 6 months–1 year 15 14.4

bias: People who post are not everyone who quits. People who find it easy have little reason to post.
People post more when it is hard, so the curve likely runs higher than for quitters in general.
Later days are mostly milestone posts; people who slipped earlier are no longer counted there.
Scores come from AI readers of the posts, not from the writers themselves.

planSteps.title: Name what it does for you
planSteps.text: Identify what beliefs are driving your porn use. Find a positive reframe (the table above).
do: Still watching? Don’t quit yet. For the next few days, watch the way you normally do.
When one of the thoughts above comes up, do the step under it. Don’t go looking for it.
Already stopped? Don’t start watching again to do this step: write it from memory.
Before each time, write one line: the hour, where you are, what you felt just before.
After, one more line: what it gave you, and what it cost.
Then write down what porn does for you: stress relief, sleep, boredom, loneliness.
Each one is a belief. Start with the beliefs above.
Circle what repeats. Those hours and feelings are what your swaps are for.

planSteps.title: Find your 80% swaps
planSteps.text: Find “80%” alternatives: if you think porn use relaxes you, find something that meets 80% of that need, like reading, a show, or talking to a friend.
do: Late nights: the phone charges outside the bedroom.
Stress or boredom: a walk, a workout, a call with a friend.
Loneliness: put that energy into meeting real people.
A craving that won’t let go: a cold shower, then out of the room.
The laptop lives on a desk or a shared table, never in bed.
A swap only has to cover 80% of the need. It doesn’t have to feel as good.

proof.text: Men keeping 104 porn-quit journals, most calling themselves addicted, built exercise, going out, meditating and better sleep into their days.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
refs.quote: Day-to-day behavioral strategies (e.g., exercising, meditating, socializing, keeping busy, going out more often, and having a healthier sleep routine) were incorporated as part of an overall lifestyle change

planSteps.title: Pick the date. Three months, one thing.
planSteps.text: Set a date (some days or weeks ahead) and make this the one thing for the next three months. Every day you keep that promise to yourself is a complete success. If you slip, go back through steps 1–3.
do: Pick the date, a few days or weeks out, and tell one person. Already off it? Today is your date.
Before that day, install a blocker and give the password to someone else.
From that date, porn is the one thing for three months. Leave the rest of your life as it is.
Plan the first week of the three months evening by evening: where you’ll be at the hours you circled in step 1.
Mark every kept day on a calendar.
Slip? The same day, go back through steps 1–3 on paper: what came just before it, a swap for that hour, your promise renewed. Don’t start the three months over.

proof.text: In 104 men’s porn-quit journals, the outside help that seemed to matter most was support from other people and being accountable to someone.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
refs.quote: social support and accountability appeared to be the external resources that were most instrumental to members’ ability to sustain abstinence

planSteps.title: Live as if you’ve already quit
planSteps.text: From that day on, act, think and feel as if you have already quit. Ask yourself: “why would I watch porn, when I’ve been porn-free for a year already and I enjoy my life so much more now?”
do: When shame hits after a slip, do what a man who doesn’t watch porn would do next: shower, get dressed, get out of the house.
After a slip, keep the count going: you lost a day, not the three months.
When the urge comes, name it: “there is a craving.” Not “I want to.” Never “I need to.”
Don’t fight the thought. Let the craving sit there and carry on with what you were doing.
When it pulls, answer the way a man who doesn’t watch porn would: “I don’t watch that.”
Count the evenings you get back, not the days you missed.

proof.text: In men’s porn-quit journals, pushing the thought of porn away was common, and some found over time that it backfired.

refs.cite: Fernandez DP, Kuss DJ, Griffiths MD (2021). The pornography “rebooting” experience: a qualitative analysis of abstinence journals on an online pornography abstinence forum. Archives of Sexual Behavior 50:711-728.
refs.quote: Attempting to suppress thoughts of pornography was a common cognitive strategy used, but some members realized over time that thought suppression was counterproductive

planSteps.title: Get help that works (optional)
planSteps.text: Get help (optional): friends, family, therapy, rehab, 12-step groups, or 1-on-1 help from me.
do: Look for a therapist who uses CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) or ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy): talk therapies that work on the habit and the urges, not on blame.
Help is a tool for steps 1 to 4, not a replacement for them.
Embarrassed to ask? A therapist who works with this has heard it all before.
Try a group, online or in a room. Go a few times, and keep going only while it helps.
Don’t wait for a pill. None is proven for porn yet.
